newsitem.title: USA: NEW YORK BROKERAGE OWNER CHARGED WITH FRAUD.
newsitem.headline: NEW YORK BROKERAGE OWNER CHARGED WITH FRAUD.

text.p: The owner of New York brokerage has been charged in a federal indictment of being involved in a scheme to defraud customers through purchases of Securitek International Corp stock, prosecutors said Wednesday.
Securitek is a penny stock traded on the over-the-counter market.

The 29-count indictment, unsealed in New York on Tuesday, names Jeffrey Szur, the owner of J.S. Securities Inc, his mother Elaine Szur, and four others, who worked as supervisors for the brokerage in several area offices.

The defendants are accused of conspiracy, wire fraud, bribery, falsifying records and money laundering in connection with their alleged participation in a large-scale scheme with Bertram Slutsky, a co-conspirator, the indictment said.
The charges stem from an FBI sting operation in which agents posed as corrupt brokers willing to accept bribes for selling stock to their customers.
According to the indictment, Slutsky owned or controlled a majority of the outstanding common stock of Securitek.
The indictment also alleges that J.S. Securities did not disclose the full amount of compensation that persons associated with the firm were receiving for selling Securitek stock, as required.
Securitek's stock closed Tuesday unchanged at 6.25 cents, its 52-week low, on trading of 7,500 shares. That compares with a year high of $1.38.
Securitek, formerly called U.S. Asset Corp, designs and markets security and surveillance systems for the military, government and law enforcement agencies.
It said in November it agreed to buy the assets of Barrett & Blandford Associates Inc, a maker of military night-vision products, for about $500,000.
Jeffrey Szur faces 110 years in prison and $7.5 million in fines if convicted. His mother faces 95 years in prison and $6.25 million in fines, if convicted.
The other four defendants face between 60 and 70 years in prison and fines in excess of $2 million if convicted.
